newsitem.title: UK: Despite publicized accidents, air travel getting safer.
newsitem.headline: Despite publicized accidents, air travel getting safer.

text.p: Your jet sinks toward the runway, hits the ground a bit harder than you expect, but it is down safely and your vacation can begin.

If you breathe a sigh of relief and offer up a silent prayer for your safe arrival, that is understandable. Even massive Boeing 747s carrying up to 400 passengers can seem vulnerable in the air, battered by winds and shaken by turbulence.

But relax. Travel by air is safer than ever and getting "Although annual figures can vary considerably and despite 1996's poor results, fatal accident rates are still improving, perhaps halving every 10 years," said Paul Hayes, director of aviation information at Airclaims consultancy.
Hayes was commenting on Airclaims' latest data, which show there was only one major loss of a Western-built airliner in the first half of 1997.
This crash, of a China Southern Airlines Boeing 737-300 while landing in a thunderstorm at Shenzhen May 8, killed 33 passengers and two crew members.
This compares with 401 deaths from the crashes of four major Western-built jets in the first half of 1996.
Last year's record was deadly, with 1,187 passengers killed -- the worst year in civil aviation history.

Notable was TWA's Boeing 747 Flight 800, which exploded while climbing over Long Island, New York, claiming 230 lives. There also was the in-flight collision between a Saudi Arabia Airlines Boeing 747 and a Kazakh Airlines Ilyushin Il-76 freighter near New Delhi, India, which killed 349 people.

But despite this carnage, which dominated the news and raised public apprehension, the number of plane crashes has remained fairly constant over the last 20 years. Despite the increase in fatalities, travel by air has become statistically safer.

"We would now be getting an average of about 15,000 passenger fatalities per year if accident rates had not improved since the early 1960s. Flying is 20 times safer now than in the early years of jets," said Hayes.
Flight International, the weekly industry magazine, says the latest figures are encouraging but warns against any premature euphoria.

"Airline accident figures for the first six months of 1997 will encourage the commercial air transport industry because the trends now show a gradual flight-safety improvement in absolute terms," David Learmount, Flight's operations and safety editor, said in a recent article

"Six months is too short a period to be taken as a serious indicator, however, and the airlines are not attempting to deceive themselves that a major battle has been won, let alone the war," Learmount said.
The technology of flight is impressively reliable and so-called black boxes often survive to provide detailed information for experts seeking reasons for the relatively rare crash.
But some unsolved incidents provide a nagging reminder that it is still possible for airliners to drop out of the sky for no apparent reason.

A USAir Boeing 737 dived on approach to Pittsburgh in 1994, killing 132 people. A United Airlines 737 crashed in similar circumstances in Colorado Springs, Colo., in 1991, claiming 25 lives. Both crashes still puzzle investigators.
And the crash of TWA 800 has not been definitively solved, although experts now believe an explosion in a fuel tank ignited by sparks was the most likely cause.
Airclaims' Hayes said airline safety experts have been seeking to identify the phases of flight that are the most hazardous.
"A high proportion of accidents were categorized as 'controlled flight into the ground,'" he said.
These crashes occurred when navigational errors by air crew or lack of concentration led to planes flying directly into high ground or mountains. They were invariably fatal.

"Safety experts like the NTSB (National Transportation Safety Board) are increasingly considering the whole culture of an airline and its management, looking at the environment in which they operate and (in which) crews perform tasks, to see if this can have an impact on safety," said Hayes.
